summary: This document specified how to carry an H.263 video bitstream inside RTP packets. It was standards-track and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2190 explains how to send H.263 video over RTP, the protocol that carries real-time media over IP. Each packet holds a short header followed by an untouched piece of the video bitstream. The header repeats what the decoder needs to know, such as which coding options the picture used, so a decoder can pick up again after a packet is lost.

subtitle: How to cut an H.263 video bitstream into RTP packets, with three payload header sizes to choose from.

tldr.problem: A video encoder produces one continuous bitstream, but the network delivers separate packets that can be lost, so the bitstream has to be cut into pieces a decoder can still use after a loss.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries a small H.263 payload header before the untouched video bitstream. Three header modes exist: a four-byte one that starts packets at group-of-blocks boundaries, and eight- and twelve-byte ones that start them at macroblock boundaries.
tldr.outcome: The header repeats the coding options and the decoder state needed to resynchronise, so a decoder can carry on after a lost packet. The format applies to the 1996 version of H.263 and RFC 2190 is Historic today.

facts.label: Macroblock
facts.value: four 8x8 luminance blocks and two chrominance blocks

today: RFC 2190 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. The document was published in September 1997 as a Standards Track protocol and covers the 1996 version of H.263.

sections.title: What This Payload Format Does
sections.content:
This document describes a scheme to packetize an H.263 video stream for transport using RTP. H.263 itself is defined by ITU-T Recommendation H.263 for video coding at very low data rates. RTP is defined by the Internet Engineering Task Force to provide end-to-end network transport functions suitable for applications transmitting real-time data over multicast or unicast network services.

Three modes are defined for the H.263 payload header. An RTP packet can use any of the three, depending on the desired network packet size and the H.263 encoding options in use. The shortest payload header, mode A, supports fragmentation at Group of Block, or GOB, boundaries. The two longer headers, modes B and C, support fragmentation at macroblock boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: H.263 compresses video into one long stream of bits. RTP sends data in separate numbered packets, and any of them can be lost. This RFC works out where to cut the video stream so that a lost packet costs as little as possible.

sections.title: Picture Formats, GOBs and Macroblocks
sections.content:
The RFC defines the picture formats that H.263 uses. CIF, the Common Intermediate Format, has 352 by 288 pixels for luminance and 176 by 144 for chrominance. QCIF, the quarter CIF source format, has 176 by 144 for luminance and 88 by 72 for chrominance. Sub-QCIF has 128 by 96 for luminance and 64 by 48 for chrominance. 4CIF has 704 by 576 for luminance and 352 by 288 for chrominance, and 16CIF has 1408 by 1152 for luminance and 704 by 576 for chrominance.

A GOB, a Group of Blocks, consists of k times 16 lines, where k depends on the picture format: k is 1 for QCIF, CIF and sub-QCIF, k is 2 for 4CIF and k is 4 for 16CIF. A macroblock contains four blocks of luminance and the spatially corresponding two blocks of chrominance, and each block is 8 by 8 pixels. There are eleven macroblocks in a GOB in QCIF format and twenty two in a GOB in CIF format.
sections.plainLanguage: An H.263 picture is built from rows of macroblocks, each macroblock being a small square of the picture. A GOB is a horizontal band of macroblocks, and the bands are the natural place to cut the bitstream into packets.

sections.title: Why Packetizing H.263 Is Hard
sections.content:
H.263 is based on ITU-T Recommendation H.261. It uses similar techniques to reduce temporal and spatial redundancy, but several differences between the two affect the design of packetization schemes. H.263 supports four negotiable coding options that can be used in any combination: Advanced Prediction, PB-frames, Syntax-based Arithmetic Coding, and Unrestricted Motion Vectors.

Advanced Prediction lets some macroblocks in a frame use one or four motion vectors, which makes recovery from packet loss difficult because more redundant information has to be preserved at the beginning of a packet. PB-frames code two frames, a P frame and a B frame, into one bitstream with macroblocks from the two frames interleaved. A macroblock from the P frame and its counterpart from the B frame must be treated together, because each B macroblock is coded from the corresponding P macroblock, and a means must be provided to ensure that the two frames are rendered in the right order. If part of that combined bitstream is lost, it affects both frames and possibly more. Syntax-based Arithmetic Coding codes the run-value pairs produced by quantizing DCT coefficients differently from Huffman codes while preserving the macroblock hierarchy, but its context variables are only synchronized after fixed-length codes, so a fragmentation that starts at variable-length codes is hard to decode after a packet loss unless all the context values travel in every payload header. Unrestricted Motion Vectors allow a larger range of motion vectors than normal. All four options are signalled in the H.263 payload header.

Each picture is divided into GOBs, numbered by a vertical scan that starts at the top GOB and ends at the bottom one. Each GOB can have a fixed GOB header, but its use is optional, and when it is present it may or may not start on a byte boundary; byte alignment can be achieved by bit stuffing but is not required by the H.263 bitstream specification. Because a GOB is coded with finer granularity than in H.261 while keeping the same source format, there is more flexibility for packetization than H.261 allows.

Motion vectors are the hardest part. They are coded differentially with variable-length codes, and H.263 predicts them from one or three candidates depending on whether the GOB header is present. If the GOB header is present, motion vectors are coded with reference to macroblocks in the current GOB only. If it is absent, three motion vectors must be available to decode one macroblock, and two of them may come from the previous GOB. To decode a whole inter-coded GOB, all the motion vectors for the previous GOB must be available, or the predictors themselves must be present. When a packet starts at a macroblock and the previous packet is lost, that information is gone, and duplicating it at the start of the packet would be far too expensive in bandwidth. The RFC therefore strongly recommends using the GOB header for every GOB at the beginning of a packet.

Some cross-GOB dependencies cannot be fixed this way. In 16CIF and 4CIF pictures a GOB holds more than one row of macroblocks, so if a GOB does not fit in one RTP packet and the first packet holding the GOB header is lost, the macroblocks in the second packet cannot compute their motion vectors correctly. When OBMC, Overlapped Block Motion Compensation, is used in Advanced Prediction mode, motion compensation for some macroblocks in one GOB can use motion vectors from the previous GOB whatever the GOB header says.

One more piece of information is needed. H.261 codes a macroblock address with a variable-length code, but H.263 does not code it explicitly. The address within a GOB is nevertheless necessary to recover from packet loss when fragmenting at macroblock boundaries, so it must be included in the payload header for the modes that allow that kind of fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Video compression makes each part of the picture depend on the part before it, so losing a packet can break everything after it. H.263 has several optional tricks that make this worse. The RFC works through each one and explains what the header must carry so a decoder can recover.

sections.title: Carrying the Stream in RTP
sections.content:
When transmitting H.263 video streams over the Internet, the output of the encoder can be packetized directly. For every video frame, the H.263 bitstream itself is carried in the RTP payload without alteration, including the picture start code and the entire picture header, in addition to any fixed-length codes and variable-length codes. The framing information specified by H.223 is not added, so multiplexing audio and video signals in the same packet is not accommodated; UDP and RTP provide a much more efficient way to achieve multiplexing.

RTP does not guarantee a reliable and orderly delivery service, so a packet might get lost in the network. To achieve a best-effort recovery from packet loss, the decoder needs help to carry on decoding the packets it did receive, so it is desirable to be able to process each packet independently of the others. Each packet therefore carries some frame-level information, such as the source format and flags for the optional features, to assist the decoder in operating correctly and efficiently in the presence of packet loss. Those flags also give session management tools information about the coding options used in the bitstream.

Three fields of the RTP fixed header are used. The Marker bit is set to 1 when the current packet carries the end of the current frame, and to 0 otherwise. The Payload Type shall specify the H.263 video payload format using the value given by the RTP profile in use, for example RFC 1890. The Timestamp encodes the sampling instant of the video frame in the packet; it may be the same on successive packets when one video frame occupies more than one packet. For H.263 video streams the timestamp is based on a 90 kHz clock, the same clock as for H.261 video streams.

Each RTP packet is laid out as the RTP fixed header, then the H.263 payload header, then the standard H.263 compressed bitstream. The size of the payload header depends on the mode in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The video data itself is copied into the packet unchanged. Only a small header is added, and that header repeats the details a decoder needs if it misses a packet. The ordinary RTP header does its usual job of marking the last packet of a frame and stamping the frame's time.

sections.title: The Three Payload Header Modes
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carries only one H.263 video packet, and the payload header is always present. Three formats are defined. In mode A a four-byte payload header precedes the compressed bitstream, and the bitstream is packetized on a GOB boundary or a picture boundary. In mode B an eight-byte header is used and each packet starts at a macroblock boundary, without the PB-frames option. In mode C a twelve-byte header is defined, to support fragmentation at macroblock boundaries for frames coded with the PB-frames option.

The mode of each header is indicated by the F and P fields. Packets of different modes can be intermixed. All client applications are required to be able to receive packets in any mode, but decoding mode C packets is optional, because the PB-frames feature itself is optional. The RFC draws the headers as rows of 32-bit words, each word transmitted in network byte order, with the most significant bit of a numeric field at the left.

The mode A header carries F and P, the start and end bit positions, the source format, four one-bit flags for the optional features, a reserved field, and the three PB-frames fields. The start bit position says how many most significant bits to ignore in the first data byte, and the end bit position how many least significant bits to ignore in the last one. The source format is the source format value defined by H.263, giving the resolution of the current picture. The four flags say whether the picture used inter-coded macroblocks, Unrestricted Motion Vectors, Syntax-based Arithmetic Coding and Advanced Prediction. The reserved field must be set to zero.

The mode B header keeps the same leading fields and replaces the PB-frames fields with the quantizer for the first macroblock coded at the start of the packet, the GOB number in effect at that point, the address of the first macroblock within its GOB counted from zero in scan order, and four motion vector predictors of seven bits each, for the first macroblock and for its third block under Advanced Prediction. The mode C header is the mode B header plus the PB-frames fields and a 19-bit reserved field, which must also be set to zero.

Mode A is used for packets starting with a GOB or the picture start code, and mode B or C whenever a packet has to start at a macroblock boundary, which is necessary for GOBs larger than the network packet size. The RFC strongly recommends mode A whenever possible, because its header is smaller, which cuts transmission overhead and can save a lot at very low data rates or small packet sizes. Mode A also simplifies recovery after packet loss: the decoder's internal state can be recovered at GOB boundaries instead of having to synchronise with macroblocks, and GOB headers and the picture start code are easy to identify, so their presence will normally make an H.263 decoder resynchronise.
sections.plainLanguage: Three header sizes are available. The smallest lets a packet start only at a group boundary; the larger ones allow a packet to start in the middle of a group, at a macroblock, which is needed when a group is too big for one packet. The RFC recommends the small header whenever it fits, because it costs less and is easier to recover from.

sections.title: Limitations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that security issues are addressed by RTP itself, and that this memo brings up no additional security issues.

It also records one limitation. The packetization method described applies to the 1996 version of H.263, and it may not be applicable to bitstreams with features added after that.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in this format adds a security problem beyond the ones RTP already has. The one limit is age: the scheme was written for the 1996 edition of H.263 and may not fit later additions to the video coding standard.

cells: GOB boundary or picture start code

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Flag bit. F=0 means mode A; F=1 means mode B or mode C depending on the P bit.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: PB-frames flag. Zero means a normal I or P frame, one means PB-frames. With F=1 it selects mode B when zero and mode C when one.

fields.name: SBIT
fields.desc: Start bit position: how many most significant bits to ignore in the first data byte.

fields.name: EBIT
fields.desc: End bit position: how many least significant bits to ignore in the last data byte.

fields.name: SRC
fields.desc: Source format, bits 6, 7 and 8 of the H.263 picture type field. Gives the resolution of the current picture.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Picture coding type, bit 9 of the H.263 picture type field. Zero is intra-coded, one is inter-coded.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Unrestricted Motion Vector option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Syntax-based Arithmetic Coding option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Advanced Prediction option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be set to zero.

fields.name: DBQ
fields.desc: Differential quantization parameter for the B frame, used when the PB-frames option is on. Set to zero otherwise.

fields.name: TRB
fields.desc: Temporal reference for the B frame. Set to zero when the PB-frames option is not used.

fields.name: TR
fields.desc: Temporal reference for the P frame. Set to zero when the PB-frames option is not used.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Flag bit. F=1 with P=0 selects mode B.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: PB-frames flag. Mode B is used only without the PB-frames option.

fields.name: SBIT
fields.desc: Start bit position: how many most significant bits to ignore in the first data byte.

fields.name: EBIT
fields.desc: End bit position: how many least significant bits to ignore in the last data byte.

fields.name: SRC
fields.desc: Source format, bits 6, 7 and 8 of the H.263 picture type field. Gives the resolution of the current picture.

fields.name: QUANT
fields.desc: Quantization value for the first macroblock coded at the start of the packet. Set to 0 if the packet begins with a GOB header.

fields.name: GOBN
fields.desc: GOB number in effect at the start of the packet.

fields.name: MBA
fields.desc: Address within the GOB of the first macroblock in the packet, counted from zero in scan order.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be set to zero.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Picture coding type. Zero is intra-coded, one is inter-coded.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Unrestricted Motion Vector option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Syntax-based Arithmetic Coding option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the Advanced Prediction option was set in the current picture header.

fields.name: HMV1
fields.desc: Horizontal motion vector predictor for the first macroblock, in half pixel resolution as a two's complement number.

fields.name: VMV1
fields.desc: Vertical motion vector predictor for the first macroblock, in half pixel resolution as a two's complement number.

fields.name: HMV2
fields.desc: Horizontal motion vector predictor for block number 3 of the first macroblock, used with the advanced prediction option.

fields.name: VMV2
fields.desc: Vertical motion vector predictor for block number 3 of the first macroblock, used with the advanced prediction option.
